🔴ExxonMobil has spent millions of dollars on the local community, yet the people living next to its carbon project are protesting
Exxon's strange social responsibility: millions spent, one unhappy community
✍️Naft Khabar:
🚨ExxonMobil has spent money on the local community, provided equipment to emergency responders, established scholarships, and its employees have put in thousands of hours of volunteer work. On paper, nearly every element of a corporate social responsibility program is there. And yet, some of the people who are supposed to live alongside one of the company's largest carbon storage projects in Texas are protesting, saying their concerns about water, safety, and the future of their community have not been heard enough.
🚨What makes the story of ExxonMobil's Rose project so intriguing is precisely this contradiction: a company that spends money on its host community, while that same community has questions and objections about its project.
🚨Over the course of 13 years, roughly 53 million tons of carbon dioxide are set to be injected deep underground in southeastern Texas. Exxon says the Rose CCS project is part of the solution for cutting emissions from America's heavy industries. But local residents have a simpler question: if the carbon from big industries is going to be buried beneath our land, who can guarantee our water, our safety, and the future of this region?
🚨The Texas Railroad Commission, the state body that regulates oil, gas, and underground storage, issued the project permit in September by a two-to-one vote. The key detail was that the dissenting vote came not from an environmental group, but from one of the commission's own three members.

In sum, in recent years we have not treated our water resources properly and have created many problems in our country's environmental and territorial foundations, the most important of which can be summarized as: the drying up of the country's important lakes and wetlands such as Hor al-Azim, Shadegan, Gavkhouni, Jazmurian, Hamoun, and Lake Urmia; the severe drop in groundwater levels across the country's important plains and land subsidence; the growth of dust centers; the problem of aquatic and terrestrial life and pollution in the downstream stretches of rivers; and seawater intrusion into rivers. Therefore, now that there is a possibility of a large volume of water falling from the sky, we can welcome it with two approaches. One approach, rooted in fear and threat, is to focus all our efforts on safely channeling the huge volume of water to the sea, which may also alleviate a few of the above-mentioned problems along its path. But the other approach focuses on making the utmost beneficial use of this yield so that we can solve many of the above-mentioned problems beforehand. Pursuing the second approach, which is certainly in the interest of our country's present and future, requires precise planning, structural works, and, more broadly, a change in how we view this phenomenon. Planning for flood spreading, maximum recharge of aquifers in the country's critical plains, the planned channeling of floods toward wetlands, channeling floods toward dust centers, and finally the safe channeling of floods toward downstream areas and the sea — all of this can be seen as the result of shifting our view of El Niño from a curse to a blessing, and can turn our fear of facing it into an opportunity. 📳 Baspar Exclusive/ When ships sit idle, what happens beneath the water's surface? Why has the prolonged stoppage of ships in the Persian Gulf once again brought the issue of marine coatings to the fore?🔸 Baspar/Iran Polymer The maritime crisis in the Persian Gulf and restricted traffic along the route leading to the Strait of Hormuz is not merely a matter of scheduling, loading, or cargo delivery. For a ship that remains stationary in the water for weeks or months, some of the most significant changes take place where they cannot be seen from the deck: below the water's surface. The hull surface, in constant contact with seawater — under conditions where the ship has been deprived of its normal movement — enters a biological and hydrodynamic process that can, once the ship returns to its route, manifest as reduced speed, increased engine load, higher fuel consumption, and diminished voyage efficiency.✍️ Golrokh Fard Zolfaghari, PhD student in Polymer Engineering 🔸 A field example of this situation has also been observed with one of the Hapag-Lloyd ships. After six to eight weeks in water at a temperature of about 30 degrees Celsius, this ship encountered a significant amount of biofouling. Biofouling and barnacles had covered the entire surface of the propeller and most of the ship's vertical surfaces, and about 40 percent of the underwater hull surface was also covered with this growth. The company's CEO stated that the amount of biofouling that had developed was such that the ship was forced to move at a lower speed when passing through the Strait of Hormuz.🔸 According to SAFETY4SEA, increased biofouling can lead to reduced ship speed, higher fuel consumption, increased engine load, and greater emissions of pollutants. entry.title: [darvishnameh] The play "Cyrus" is not a return to the past for me; it is looking at today…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

The play "Cyrus" is not a return to the past for me; it is looking at today through the mirror of history. In writing this play, rather than seeking to construct a mythical figure of Cyrus, I have thought about a human being who, amid power, violence, and fear, faces a difficult choice: the sword or the word. History, for me, is not a mass of names and conquests; it is the memory of the people who lived in it; people who were afraid, who loved, who betrayed, who stood firm, and who made choices at fateful moments. "Cyrus" is an attempt to hear the silenced voices of these very people; to see the human beings who have sometimes been forgotten behind the great names of history. As a director, too, I have not wanted to reconstruct history; I have wanted to summon it into the present; so that perhaps we may realize that the distance between that era and our era is not as far as we think. "Cyrus" is not the narrative of a conqueror; it is the search for a human being who wants to take power beyond the mere meaning of domination. Perhaps that is why, for me, "Cyrus" is more about the possibility of remaining human in the midst of power than about the past.#نادر_برهانی_مرند@moaser_theater
